passage: Darshan was sure the new group member was honest. "Look at him, palms open, he's got nothing to hide." I'm Urmila, and I was sitting right there. Madhav had said, "Trust me, I'll do the slides," hands turned up like a shopkeeper's. Darshan relaxed. I watched, though, and thought: open hands feel friendly, but they're only one clue. So I asked, "Which slides, and by when?" Madhav said, "The last three, by Friday," and wrote it down. That answer was more useful than the palms. Darshan shrugged. "Fair. I just liked how open he looked." I said it was a nice sign, not proof.

qa.q: What did Madhav say he would do for the group?
qa.a: He said, "Trust me, I'll do the slides."

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when he decided Madhav was honest?
qa.a: Darshan felt reassured and trusting because Madhav's palms were open. Urmila suggests that Darshan was leaning on one cue.

qa.q: What small step made the situation clearer?
qa.a: Urmila asked which slides and by when, and Madhav gave a clear answer. Concrete details are more useful than a single gesture.

qa.q: How does Urmila see open palms differently from Darshan?
qa.a: Urmila treats open palms as a friendly sign that isn't proof of honesty. Darshan almost took them as the whole answer.

grounding: A teenager reads open palms as honesty, but they are only one cue and not proof.

passage:
Monday. Madhav held out his open palms and said, "I'll return your book tomorrow, promise." Darshan smiled. Open hands, honest face. Fine.
Wednesday. No book. Madhav apologised and said he'd forgotten it at home. He looked sorry, palms open again. Darshan felt a small jolt of doubt and then felt bad for it.
Friday. Darshan said, "Let's say a day and time. Tomorrow at ten, at the gate?" Madhav wrote it on his hand. The book came back on time. Darshan thought that the open palms had been friendly but the plan was what worked.

qa.q: What did Madhav promise on Monday?
qa.a: He promised to return the book tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Darshan feel when the book didn't come on Wednesday?
qa.a: Darshan felt a small jolt of doubt and then felt bad for doubting. Darshan had trusted Madhav's open palms and now wasn't sure what to make of the forgetting.

qa.q: What worked for Darshan after the book was late?
qa.a: Darshan agreed a day and time, at ten at the gate, and Madhav wrote it down. A clear plan helped more than reading a gesture.

qa.q: How might Madhav have felt when he forgot the book?
qa.a: Madhav looked sorry and probably felt embarrassed. His open palms showed friendliness, but he had simply forgotten.

grounding: A teenager reads open palms as honesty and learns it is only one cue, and a plan works better.

passage:
"Kalyani, you think if someone shows you open palms, they're honest? Let your Raghav Thatha tell you something.
When I was sixteen, a senior boy wanted to borrow my new cycle. He held both hands open, palms up, and said, 'I promise, I'll bring it back by evening.' He looked so sincere, I believed him.
He didn't bring it back that evening, or the next. After three days, I told my father, and he went with me to the boy's house. The cycle was there, with a flat tyre and a bent pedal.
Open palms made me trust him. But they weren't proof. Now I look at what people do, not just their hands."

qa.q: How many days passed before Raghav told his father?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: What was young Raghav feeling when the senior showed open palms?
qa.a: He felt trusting and reassured, believing the open palms meant the senior was honest.

qa.q: What choice inside the story helped Raghav get the cycle back?
qa.a: Raghav chose to tell his father, who went with him to the boy's house.

qa.q: How might the senior have seen his own promise?
qa.a: The senior may not have taken the promise seriously, using open palms to seem trustworthy without meaning it.

grounding: A grandfather recalls trusting open palms as honesty and learning they are only one cue, not proof.

passage:
Ten minutes before the maths exam, Asif's calculator was missing. He turned to Jomon, who sat next to him. "Did you take it?"
Jomon held both hands out, palms open. "I swear, I didn't touch it."
Asif wanted to believe him. The open palms looked honest. But open palms can be faked too.
He didn't argue. He checked his bag again, then ran to the science lab where he'd had the last class. The calculator was on the bench.
He came back panting. "Sorry. Found it in the lab."
Jomon laughed. "Told you."
Asif sat down. The palms had been true this time, but checking was what proved it.

qa.q: Where did Asif find his calculator?
qa.a: On the bench in the science lab.

qa.q: What was Asif thinking when Jomon showed open palms?
qa.a: Asif felt torn: he wanted to believe the palms meant honesty, but was unsure since palms alone aren't proof.

qa.q: What did Asif do that was fair?
qa.a: He didn't accuse Jomon further and checked the facts himself, which proved Jomon was telling the truth.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt when Asif asked if he took it?
qa.a: Jomon was probably a bit hurt at first but relieved when the calculator was found.

grounding: Before an exam, a teenager reads a peer's open palms as honesty but checks the facts, since palms are not proof.

passage:
On Saturday, a new family moved into the flat opposite Dhruv's. The son, Samir, stood in the doorway with open palms. "Hey! Want to play cricket downstairs later?"
Dhruv felt welcomed. The open hands made Samir seem easy to trust.
Later that day, at the market, a man selling earphones held his palms open too. "Original, one hundred percent! Trust me!"
Dhruv laughed to himself. Same gesture, but the earphones looked cheap and fake.
He told Samir about it while they played. Samir grinned. "So you trust me because of my hands?"
"And because you actually brought a bat," Dhruv said.
Open palms could mean welcome, but they weren't proof of anything on their own.

qa.q: What did Samir invite Dhruv to play?
qa.a: Cricket downstairs.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when Samir showed open palms?
qa.a: Dhruv felt welcomed and at ease, reading the open hands as friendly.

qa.q: What did Dhruv realise at the market?
qa.a: That open palms can also be used to seem honest when selling something fake, so the gesture alone isn't proof.

qa.q: How might Samir see Dhruv's comment about his hands?
qa.a: Samir found it funny and was glad his actions, like bringing a bat, backed up his welcome.

grounding: A teenager reads open palms as welcome from a neighbour but sees the same gesture used by a seller, learning it isn't proof.

passage:
"I swear, Aman, I didn't tell anyone about your audition." Parveen held both palms open towards him. "Look. Nothing to hide."
Amandeep studied her hands. "Mehul says you told him."
"Mehul says a lot of things."
"You're doing the open-palms thing. Like those videos say honest people do."
"Because I am honest!"
"Maybe. But anyone can open their hands." Amandeep sighed. "I don't want to decide from your hands. Did you tell anyone at all? Even by accident?"
Parveen lowered her hands slowly. "I told my sister. At home. Mehul was on a video call with her."
"So not on purpose."
"No. But it got out because of me. I'm sorry."
Amandeep nodded. "Thanks for telling me what really happened."

qa.q: What had Amandeep kept secret?
qa.a: An audition.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling while studying Parveen's hands?
qa.a: He felt hurt and suspicious after hearing from Mehul, but also unsure, and didn't want to judge from her hands alone.

qa.q: Why was Amandeep's question better than trusting the open palms?
qa.a: Open palms are one cue, not proof either way; a specific question brought out what had actually happened.

qa.q: How might Parveen have felt when asked "Even by accident?"
qa.a: Parveen probably felt guilty, and relieved to be given a way to tell the whole truth, since the leak wasn't on purpose.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager treating open palms as one cue, not proof of honesty, and asking a clear question instead.
